aide.title: Help
aide.intro: Bobi.Tools hosts tools shared as plugins. Install them on demand; each tool comes with its own interface.
aide.concept_body: Each tool declares its execution mode in its manifest:
aide.runtime_inprocess: runs inside the application itself (lightweight utilities, front-only or a small Python backend).
aide.runtime_docker: runs in an isolated Docker container with its own dependencies. The app proxies calls to the container.
aide.use_launcher: The home page lists every tool you can access, grouped by section.
aide.use_focus: Each tool has a stable (bookmarkable) address, for example
aide.use_test: Test mode (from the section) lets you switch quickly between tools.
aide.admin_install: Settings → Plugins: import/export a .bobitool package, manage versions, enable/disable.
aide.admin_access: Per-tool access control: choose which roles may open each tool.
aide.admin_audit: Audit log: who did what, in which tool.
aide.author_body: A tool is a folder under plugins/:
aide.mail_intro: The Mail service lets any tool send an email — typically to raise an alert. The tool supplies the message; the service centralises SMTP configuration and handles delivery.
aide.mail_send_inprocess: In-process tool (backend.py): call the helper ctx.send_mail(subject, body, to=…). With no recipient, the message goes to the default alert recipients configured in settings.
aide.mail_send_docker: Docker tool: call the HTTP route, authenticated by the shared token (Settings → Mail):
aide.mail_send_async: Sending is asynchronous and best-effort: the call returns immediately and never fails loudly; the outcome (success/failure) is recorded in the audit log under "Service Mail".
aide.mail_config_body: Settings → Mail tab: enable the service, fill in the SMTP server (host, port, STARTTLS/SSL/none security), credentials, sender, default alert recipients and the Docker-tools token. The "Send a test" button validates the configuration immediately.
aide.ntfy_intro: The Notifications service hosts a ntfy server (self-hosted, in a Docker container) that lets any tool push a notification to subscribed phones and browsers, over the LAN or VPN. The tool supplies the message; the service centralises the server hosting and authentication, and handles publishing.
aide.ntfy_send_inprocess: In-process tool (backend.py): call the helper ctx.notify(message, topic=…, title=…, priority=…, tags=…). With no topic, the notification goes to the default topic configured in settings. Priority accepts min/low/default/high/max (or 1 to 5); tags (comma-separated) can be ntfy emojis (warning, camera…).
aide.ntfy_send_docker: Docker tool: call the HTTP route, authenticated by the shared token (Settings → Notifications):
aide.ntfy_send_async: Publishing is asynchronous and best-effort: the call returns immediately and never fails loudly; the outcome (success/failure) is recorded in the audit log under "Service ntfy".
aide.ntfy_subscribe_body: On the phone, install the ntfy app (iOS/Android), point it at the server public URL (Settings → Notifications) and subscribe to the desired topic. A browser can also subscribe via the server URL. In "closed" mode (deny-all), subscribing requires the admin account; in "open subscribe" mode (read-only), any device on the LAN/VPN can subscribe and only publishing stays authenticated.
aide.ntfy_config_body: Settings → Notifications tab: enable the service (which starts the ntfy container), choose the LAN-published port and public URL, the default topic, the default access (closed / open subscribe), the admin username and password, and the Docker-tools token. Saving starts and provisions the server; "Send a test" validates immediately. LAN/VPN only (no Internet/TLS exposure yet).
aide.ntfy_license_body: The ntfy server (https://ntfy.sh) is dual-licensed Apache-2.0/GPLv2 and intended for self-hosting. Bobi.Tools only runs it as a separate process (official image pulled at deploy time, not redistributed) and publishes over HTTP: mere aggregation, with no conflict with Bobi.Tools' GPL-3.0 license.
settings.toolcfg_intro: Settings exposed by installed tools. Each value is specific to its tool.
settings.emberplus_hint: Ember+ provider: exposes the tools that opt in (e.g. Switch control) for read/write. Listens on a dedicated TCP port, with NO authentication — filter it at the network level. Writes are audited as "Service Ember+".
settings.emberplus_root_hint: The root is the number the controller sees the tool under. It is assigned once and never moves: installing, disabling or removing another tool does not shift it. Changing it moves the subtree on the controller; the previous number is then retired and will never be reassigned. Roots 1000 (IPG mould), 1001 (service) and 1100 (SDP) are fixed.
settings.emberplus_root_confirm: Move this subtree? The controller will see it under a new number, and any wiring on the old one must be redone. The old number will never be reassigned.
settings.emberplus_profile_hint: Shared exposed list: canonical blocks and parameters (interchangeable lanes). Each tool maps its native settings onto it. Numbering is stable — deleting an already-mapped parameter breaks VSM paths.
settings.tsl_hint: TSL UMD V5.0 sender: pushes to VSM the LABELS and a state tally for the slots, lanes and signals already exposed over Ember+ — where only the NUMBERS go on the wire, which is why the IPG assignment grid shows "11", "12" without saying which device that is. Bobi.Tools is the sender, VSM the receiver; no listening port is opened, nothing is ever written to hardware. Numbers come from the Ember+ service (same numbers on both protocols): without it this service cannot emit anything, and says so.
settings.tsl_peer_hint: UNTIL BOTH ADDRESS AND PORT ARE SET, NOTHING GOES ON THE NETWORK — even when enabled. No default is assumed: TSL 5.0 has no universally agreed port, and blind flooding of a production network would be worse than no service at all. 0.0.0.0 and 255.255.255.255 are rejected.
settings.tsl_levels_hint: Three levels of very different scale, each independently switchable. Physical signals are off by default: they amount to several thousand displays, hence as many frames per pass.
settings.tsl_plan_warn: ⚠ This plan becomes a contract as durable as the Ember+ roots the moment a VSM panel is wired to it: renumbering breaks that wiring. It can be revisited ONCE, at commissioning, and is frozen afterwards.
settings.tsl_plan_hint: The default reuses the already-frozen Ember+ plan (a block of 100 per slot: hundreds give the slot, units the signal) and only adds one screen per family. It had to: Ember+ has several independent numbering spaces (a matrix's sources, its targets, the mould's lanes) whereas TSL has only one per screen. Inputs and outputs MUST therefore stay on two distinct screens — they carry the same numbers, and one would silently overwrite the other.
settings.tsl_index_offset_hint: Added to the plan number to get the index sent. The default −1 puts the SAME integer on the TSL wire as on the Ember+ wire, which sends "displayed number − 1" because VSM re-displays +1. NOT VERIFIED against a real receiver: if the panel shows an off-by-one, this setting — and only this one — goes to 0.
settings.tsl_labels_hint: Names come from the device label in the Bobi.Tools inventory, with a manual per-index override. A NetBox integration is planned as the future source of truth; it will slot in between the two without changing what is set here.
settings.tsl_plugin_label_hint: Off (default): the template above makes the name, so the chassis identity is always in it — which is exactly what the panel lacks today. On: the connector label the plugin provides is used when it provides one. Worth knowing first: those labels carry no device name ("IP 14", "BNC 3"), so two SNPs side by side become indistinguishable, and the snp plugin gives the SAME label to its inputs and its outputs, with the wrong direction ("BNC 1 (sortie)" on an INPUT). The template's {label} field lets you combine both.
settings.tsl_overrides_hint: Label overrides, as JSON: { "2:100": "Camera 1" } targets screen 2 index 100; { "100": "Camera 1" } targets index 100 on every screen. Template fields: {device} {slot} {lane} {index} {kind} {n} {src}. In ASCII (the default) diacritics are unfolded — "Caméra" becomes "Camera", which stays readable; UTF-16LE keeps them but has not been verified against the receiver.
settings.tsl_preview_hint: Builds the frames and shows their annotated hex WITHOUT opening a socket: the only way to verify everything before a receiver exists. The three lamps read: off = unknown or not applicable, green = OK, red = fault, amber = caveat. Left = signal presence (amber when the hardware publishes a status.input_valid caveat); text = activation (amber when the crosspoint is pinned); right = PTP (amber = holdover).
settings.swp08_hint: SW-P-08 server (Pro-Bel "General Remote Control Protocol"): Bobi.Tools presents itself to the panel as a NAMED ROUTER and publishes the IPG inventory — source names, destination names and UMD labels. The opposite direction from TSL: here we LISTEN, the panel is the client, it connects and asks, we answer (16 clients at most). The mapping fits on one line: the MATRIX is the routing stage (inputs, outputs, assignment) and the LEVEL is the essence (video, audio 1, audio 2, ANC) — which avoids the thirteen receivers TSL would have needed. Numbers come from the Ember+ service and from it alone. The protocol has no authentication: filter it at the network level.
settings.swp08_port_hint: AS LONG AS THE PORT IS 0, NOTHING LISTENS — even when enabled. No default is assumed: the spec says the port is configured per installation, there is no universal value to presume.
settings.swp08_label_chars_hint: 4, 8 or 12 characters, and nothing else: the wire carries not the length but its INDEX among those three values, so a fourth cannot be negotiated. Longer labels are truncated to this width.
settings.swp08_extended_hint: Extended: 65,535 signals and 256 levels, against 1,024 and 16 in standard mode. Our plan reaches 1699 for 16 slots, so extended is not a comfort — turning it off truncates the inventory.
settings.swp08_matrix_hint: Matrix numbers as DISPLAYED (1-based); everything goes on the wire 0-based, and the conversion happens inside the service and nowhere else. The two may be identical: now that the split goes through LEVELS, they no longer separate anything. ⚠ What VSM calls a "layer" is the MATRIX, not the level (observed on the bench).
settings.swp08_levels_hint: One layer per (essence, direction) pair, then assignment. THE ORDER IS THE CONTRACT: changing it renames everything on the panel, exactly like renumbering an Ember+ root. The counters say how many labels each stage actually serves; zero everywhere means the IPG layer did not answer.
settings.swp08_write: What the panel is allowed to write
settings.swp08_assign_warn: ⚠ Allowing assignments from the panel hands it the power to RENUMBER THE WHOLE INVENTORY IN ONE CLICK: moving a device changes every one of its signal numbers (100×slot + n, on its lanes as on its connectors) and its Ember+ subtree changes path. That is an out-of-service relocation, not a production gesture. Turn it off in operation.
settings.swp08_allow_assign_hint: The "assignment" layer places a device on a slot. The write takes the same path as the Ember+ 1010 grid — two doors, one lock, so no second source of truth. When refused, an assignment order is audited and the true state is re-sent so the panel's optimistic crosspoint snaps back. Signal routing, on the other hand, is NEVER accepted over this channel: it lives on Ember+.
settings.swp08_push_names_hint: The protocol expects the router to be queried and to answer. The target panel never asks — but it PUSHES its own the same way and its table declares those commands as inbound, so we do as it does. Turning this off means sending only what is explicitly requested, which, with this panel, means sending nothing.
settings.swp08_dual_status_hint: Answer to the status command the panel issues every ten seconds. Without it, it never considers the router alive, so it never asks for names — that is what the first real trial showed. The default 2 reads as "single controller, in service"; change it only against a panel that rejects that byte.
settings.swp08_test_hint: A tiny matrix whose every byte is known: 8 sources, 8 destinations, numbered 1 to 8, obvious labels and crosspoints that fit in your head. Its purpose: to separate "is the protocol right?" from "is our model right?". The real inventory numbers from 101 up and holds 80 signals per stage; if the panel shows nothing, you cannot tell whether it is the frame format or a range outside what it expects. Here only one variable is left.
settings.swp08_test_matrix_hint: Matrix number serving the bench. It MASKS the real inventory on that matrix: leave it on a value unused in operation, or turn it off once commissioning is over.
settings.swp08_grid_warn: ⚠ REDUCING these bounds makes labels DISAPPEAR that may already be wired on the panel: whatever is no longer sent either keeps its old name on screen or blanks out, and you cannot tell which. RAISING them is safe — the additions go at the end of the grid.
settings.swp08_grid_hint: How many connectors each slot EMITS in the grids. Emission bounds, not plan bounds: the plan reserves 50 SDI and 49 IP Rx/Tx per slot, but emitting them all for sixteen slots would make 800 labels per grid when the largest machine in the inventory carries 40.
settings.swp08_labels_hint: The grids are FULL: every position of every slot carries a label, whether a device sits there or not — otherwise a half-named grid reads like a fault. Three cases, in this order: position served by an assigned device → its real name; slot occupied but without that position → the unused-position label; empty slot → the positional template. Available fields: {short} {kind} {n} {lane} {slot}. The short name comes first from the IPG layer (entered in the tool), because the name belongs to the hardware, not to the protocol.
settings.swp08_unused_hint: A template with an unknown field silently falls back to the short name alone: if a label suddenly reads just "SNP1", there is one brace too many.
settings.swp08_preview_hint: Builds the frames and shows their annotated hex WITHOUT opening a socket. This is not a comfort: the link layer is validated against the spec's own frames, but the NAME COMMANDS appear in no public spec — Issue 4b stops at the "main commands" — and come from a Companion module. Their exact layout has to be confronted on the bench, and this is where you read it.
settings.swp08_received_title: What the panel pushed to us — key "matrix/level/kind". Purely documentary: it is what lets us compare its naming plan to ours.
settings.swp08_received_none: No label received from the panel so far.
settings.mail_hint: Email (SMTP) sending service for tools — alerts and notifications. In-process tools call ctx.send_mail(...); Docker tools use POST /api/mail/send with the shared token. Sends are asynchronous and audited as "Service Mail".
settings.ntfy_hint: Self-hosted push notification server (ntfy): tools push alerts to subscribed phones/browsers on the LAN/VPN. The service HOSTS the ntfy server (Docker container) and publishes it on the chosen port. In-process tools call ctx.notify(...); Docker tools use POST /api/ntfy/publish with the shared token. Sends are asynchronous, audited as "Service ntfy". The ntfy server is licensed under Apache-2.0/GPLv2, run as mere aggregation.
settings.tool_import_hint: Drop a shared .bobitool package to install it.
settings.services_hint: Global platform facilities (not tools): versioned, separated from the core.
settings.service_import_hint: Drop a service .bobitool package to install it.
settings.service_restart_needed: Version activated — restart the app to reload the service.
settings.deploy_build_hint: The package includes DEPLOY.md, the Debian installation guide.
settings.fleet_hint: Updates the code (core + plugins/services) from one Bobi.Tools instance to another on the local network. Local state (config, database, uploads, vault key) is never overwritten, and a component missing on the target is only installed if you tick it.
settings.fleet_server_hint: Lets other instances pull this instance's code, and update it (push). They must present this token.
settings.fleet_regen_confirm: Regenerate the token? Instances using the old one will not reach this one until they are given the new one.
settings.fleet_shared_token_tip: No token of its own for this peer: this instance's token is presented.
settings.fleet_pull_tip: Update THIS instance from this peer
settings.fleet_push_tip: Update this peer from THIS instance
settings.fleet_del_confirm: Remove this instance from the list?
settings.fleet_git_warning: The target tracks a git repository: a peer update overwrites files tracked by git, and its GitHub update will then refuse to move forward until those local changes are dealt with.
settings.fleet_same_build: Same build on both sides: nothing to update, except to reinstall.
settings.fleet_new_note: New components are only installed on the target if you tick them.
settings.fleet_pull_title: Update this instance from the peer
settings.fleet_push_title: Update the peer from this instance
settings.fleet_pushing: The peer is pulling the update…
settings.deploy_rollback_confirm: Restore the latest code backup and restart?
settings.git_hint: Pulls code from the repository (single origin) as fast-forward + submodules, then restarts. Local state (config, database, uploads) is preserved. Uses the machine's git credentials.
settings.git_notgit: This instance is not a git checkout — use the .zip package import instead.
settings.git_update_confirm: Update this instance from GitHub (fast-forward + submodules) and restart?
settings.git_rollback_confirm: Revert to the commit before the last git update and restart?
settings.import_hint: For instances without Internet: import a .zip package built on another instance ("Build package" → download). No network required.
settings.import_confirm: Apply this package to this instance and restart? A backup of the current code is created first.
js.docker.start_hint: Start the tool to use it.
settings.emberplus_push_interval_hint: Interval between two re-aggregations pushed to subscribed consumers (VSM…). Only parameters that CHANGED are sent; an interval with no change emits nothing. Lowering it too far increases load on every contributing tool, polled on each cycle. 1 to 3600 s.
settings.emberplus_ui_url_hint: Published at the root of the IPG mould, so an operator at the controller knows where to reach this instance. Empty = auto-detection, which returns the default-route address — set it if the machine is multi-homed and the UI is reached through another interface.
settings.emberplus_grid_size_hint: Size of the flow grids and of the IPG mould. A lane is numbered 100×slot + local number: the number ITSELF states the slot. All lanes are always exposed to VSM (full grid), whether a device sits on the slot or not — so the panel can be wired before a device is present. Growing is safe; SHRINKING removes paths, hence any VSM config beyond. 1 to 99 slots, 1 to 50 lanes per slot.
settings.network_hint: Addresses, gateway and DNS of the machine hosting Bobi.Tools. Read only.
settings.network_host_owned: ⚠ This machine is a container: its network configuration belongs to the host, which rewrites /etc/network/interfaces and /etc/resolv.conf on every start. A change made here would not survive the next restart — it must be made on the host.
settings.network_change_hint: The address is applied immediately, then automatically REVERTED unless you confirm it — from the new address — within the time shown. That is what prevents locking yourself out: on a mistake, the machine returns to its previous configuration on its own.
settings.network_pending: Automatic revert in {s} s — reload this page from the NEW address and confirm.
settings.network_confirm_apply: Apply {a}? The machine may become unreachable at the current address. Without confirmation it will revert on its own.
settings.network_applied: Applied — confirm from the new address
settings.groups_hint: A group grants nothing by itself: it is a shared recipient for access policies (tool access, credential vaults…).
settings.emberplus_dedicated_hint: Opens a second port serving only part of the tree — for instance the multiviewer branch, so its tally is not disturbed by the full resends the rest of the park triggers. It removes nothing from the main listener: the same branches stay served there. Port 0: disabled. Changing this port restarts the provider.
settings.emberplus_delivery_hint: Only adjust on evidence. « Subtrees served at once » spares the controller from opening every node to learn its parameters (e.g. 5.2). « Elements per message » splits responses: some controllers only digest about 4 kB per message and silently truncate the rest. 0 = no splitting. Both apply live.
settings.emberplus_tally_exclusive: Stop serving these roots on the main listener
settings.emberplus_tally_exclusive_hint: Tick this ONCE the controller has moved to the dedicated listener. While unticked, the branch is served on both — that is what allows a switchover without interruption. Ticked, it disappears from the main listener: a controller still wired there for that branch will lose it. Reversible by unticking.
compte.identite_note: This information is yours: you can correct it yourself.
compte.preferences_note: They follow your account from one workstation to another and apply to you only.
compte.acces_note: Role, groups and tool access are assigned by an administrator (Settings → Users).
js.compte.pwd_differents: The two entries do not match.
settings.roles_hint: Each box applies immediately. A permission added later by a tool is only given to the roles that tool suggests, once; after that, this matrix is the reference. The administrator role always has everything.
settings.roles_mine: Careful: this matrix includes your own role. Removing a permission may prevent you from undoing it.
settings.roles_in_use: Accounts hold this role: reassign them first
settings.roles_reset_confirm: Reset this role to its original permissions?
settings.rules_hint: Restricts a tool permission to some resources (a switch, ports…), for some users, groups, roles or controllers. Three types: “Reserve” keeps resources for their beneficiaries without changing anything elsewhere; “Allow only” turns the permission into an allow-list on the whole tool; “Deny” takes an action away from those it names. Rules only apply to changes: everyone sees everything.
settings.rules_controllers_hint: Controllers are declared in Settings → Protocols → Controllers.
settings.rules_or_hint: A resource is covered if it matches any of the ticked or typed criteria.
settings.rules_no_tool: No installed tool declares permissions yet.
settings.rules_empty_some: “Some” is selected without any criterion: the rule would cover nothing.
settings.ctl_hint: Devices that drive Bobi.Tools through Ember+ or SW-P-08 (VSM…). These protocols carry no identity: the source address identifies the controller. Declared here once, they are then picked by name in scopes.
settings.ctl_in_use: Scope rules mention it: edit them first
settings.rules_mode_reserve_hint: On the chosen resources, only the beneficiaries can act. Elsewhere, nothing changes.
settings.rules_mode_allow_hint: The permission becomes an allow-list on the WHOLE tool: anyone not named by a rule of this type loses it everywhere.
settings.rules_impact_reserve: will no longer exercise it on this scope ({n}):
aide.rights_intro: Who can do what in Bobi.Tools is set at three levels, from the broadest to the finest. Only changes are controlled: everyone can always look. Scopes come in three types: Reserve, Allow only and Deny.
aide.rights_level_roles: Roles (Settings → General → Roles) — each account has a role; a matrix says which permissions each role carries. The administrator role always has everything.
aide.rights_level_perms: Tool permissions — each tool declares its actions (e.g. Switch control: “Change a port's VLAN”, “Edit a trunk”…). They appear in the same matrix, grouped by tool.
aide.rights_level_scopes: Scopes (Settings → Tools → Scopes) — rules that limit a permission to some resources (a switch, ports, a camera…) for some beneficiaries (users, groups, roles, controllers). As long as no rule mentions a permission, the role is enough.
aide.rights_reserve_body: It sets resources aside for its beneficiaries. On those resources, only they can act; everywhere else, nothing changes. Use it to say “this port belongs to this team”.
aide.rights_reserve_example:
Example: Reserve — “Change a port's VLAN” — switch Peli-03, ports 1 to 12 — for group Gallery 2.

  • Gallery 2 changes the VLAN of ports 1 to 12 of Peli-03 — and, as before, of every other port its role allows.
  • Other operators can no longer change the VLAN of ports 1 to 12 of Peli-03.
  • They keep changing the VLAN of every other port, on Peli-03 and on the other switches.
  • Renaming or shutting those ports is still possible for everyone: those are other permissions (reserve them too if needed).
aide.rights_reserve_doubt: When in doubt, the resource is treated as reserved. A bulk action that does not say which ports it touches, or a port whose role the tool cannot give, is refused to non-beneficiaries — otherwise a bulk action would be enough to bypass the reservation.
aide.rights_allow_body: It turns the permission into an allow-list over the whole tool: as soon as a rule of this type mentions a permission, only those named by such a rule can still use it — and only within their rule's scope. Keep it for sensitive actions you want to lock down entirely.
aide.rights_allow_example: Example: Allow only — HyperDeck “Format a medium” — all machines — for Pierre. From now on, Pierre is the only one (with administrators) who can format, on any machine. Everyone else has lost this action, everywhere.
aide.rights_both_body: In order: a “Deny” rule naming you blocks, no matter what. Otherwise you must pass the allow-list if there is one (“Allow only”), and be a beneficiary of the reservation if the resource is reserved. Before saving, the screen tells who loses what: read it, that is where an oversight shows.
aide.rights_ctl_body: Orders received through Ember+ and SW-P-08 follow the same rules: the controller is identified by its IP address. Declare it once (Settings → Protocols → Controllers), then tick it by name in rules. Careful: a rule on a permission VSM uses that does not name it takes that action away from it (everywhere for “Allow only”, on the scope for “Reserve”); the warning before saving points it out.
aide.rights_tips:
• An administrator is never blocked.
  • Rules only apply to changes: viewing stays open to everyone who can access the tool.
  • Each refusal is logged (action “refus_droits”) with the permission and resource involved.
  • My account (user menu) shows everyone the permissions their role gives them.
settings.rules_mode_deny_hint: The chosen beneficiaries can NOT act on these resources (on the whole tool if none is chosen). Overrides the other rules; other accounts are unaffected.
settings.rules_impact_deny: will no longer exercise it on this scope ({n}):
settings.rules_impact_deny_all: will no longer exercise it ANYWHERE ({n}):
aide.rights_deny_body: It takes an action away from those it names, on the chosen resources — or on the whole tool if none is chosen. Other accounts are unaffected. It overrides every other rule: a member of a denied group stays blocked even if they benefit from a reservation. When in doubt (a bulk action that does not say what it touches), the denial applies.
aide.rights_deny_example: Example: Deny — “Edit a trunk” and “Shut a port” — ports with role “trunk” in the plan — for group Interns. Interns keep everything else; they can no longer touch uplinks. Other operators are unaffected.
settings.images_hint: An installation without Internet access cannot build a tool's image: "Migrate" fails while downloading the base image and dependencies. Build and export the image here, on a connected machine, then import it there: "Migrate" will find the image already present and only recreate the container.
settings.images_no_docker: Docker is not responding on this host.
settings.images_build_confirm: Build the image? Internet access is required: the base image and dependencies are downloaded. Allow a few minutes; the build continues in the background.
settings.images_migrate_confirm: Recreate the tool's container on the expected image?
settings.images_import_hint: .tar.gz archive produced by "Export" on another installation (or by docker save). Only images of this installation's tools are accepted.
settings.images_import_match: image expected by the tool — click "Migrate" on its row to use it.
settings.images_import_mismatch: not the version the tool expects; "Migrate" will not use it. Expected:
